title: Nouns, Gender, and the Verb Būti
summary: Every noun is masculine or feminine and announces which by its ending; there is no article; the verb *būti* joins a subject to a predicate noun or adjective, and the adjective agrees in gender.

rules.heading: Gender
rules.statement: Every Lithuanian noun is either **masculine** or **feminine**. There is no neuter. Gender is not a statement about the thing named — a table is masculine and a book feminine for no reason outside the grammar — but it governs the form of every adjective, pronoun and participle that refers to the noun, and so must be known for each word. Fortunately the ending usually declares it.

rules.heading: The Endings of the Nominative Singular
rules.statement: In the form under which a noun is listed in the dictionary, masculine nouns end in **-as, -is, -ys** or **-us**, and feminine nouns in **-a** or **-ė**. The ending is thus a nearly reliable guide to gender. The one trap is **-is**, which belongs chiefly to masculines but also to a small closed class of feminines, of which *moteris*, woman, is the commonest.

paradigms.caption: Nominative singular endings
paradigms.footnote: Feminine in -is: moteris (woman), akis (eye), naktis (night), širdis (heart). These must be learned individually.

rules.heading: Absence of the Article
rules.statement: Lithuanian has **neither a definite nor an indefinite article**. *Namas* is at once "a house" and "the house", and which is meant is settled by the context, or, where it matters, by a demonstrative such as *tas*, that. The beginner whose own language has articles must resist the urge to supply one.

rules.heading: The Nominative Case
rules.statement: Lithuanian nouns are declined in **seven cases**, of which the first is the **nominative**. The nominative is the form given in dictionaries, and it is used for the **subject** of the sentence — the person or thing of which something is asserted. The remaining cases are taken up in the lessons that follow.

rules.heading: The Personal Pronouns
rules.statement: The personal pronouns in the nominative are given below. The third person distinguishes gender, there being a masculine and a feminine form in both numbers. Because the verb ending already shows the person, the pronoun is commonly **omitted** unless it is emphatic or needed to make clear which of two persons is meant.

paradigms.caption: Personal pronouns, nominative

rows.label: 2nd person
cells: jūs — you (more than one, or polite)

paradigms.footnote: *jie* is used of a mixed company; *jos* only where every member is feminine.

examples.note: the pronoun dropped; the ending -u says 'I' already

rules.heading: The Present Tense of Būti
rules.statement: The verb **būti**, to be, is irregular and must be learned entire. Note that the third person has **one form for both numbers and all genders** — a feature of every Lithuanian verb, not of this one alone.

paradigms.caption: būti — present tense
paradigms.footnote: Negated by prefixing ne-: nesu, nesi, nesame, nesate. The third person is irregular: **nėra**, not *neyra*.

rules.heading: The Predicate Noun and Adjective
rules.statement: When a noun or adjective is joined to the subject by *būti* and forms part of what is asserted of it, it is called a **predicate noun** or **predicate adjective**. Such a word stands in the **nominative**, exactly like the subject, because it names the subject rather than being acted upon by it.

rules.heading: Agreement of the Adjective
rules.statement: An adjective **agrees with its noun in gender**, whether it stands before the noun as an attribute or after *būti* as a predicate. Adjectives fall into three classes by their endings: **-as / -a**, **-us / -i**, and **-is / -ė**. Choosing the wrong class is the commonest error at this stage; the masculine form given in the vocabulary settles which class a given adjective belongs to.

examples.note: katė is feminine, so maža and not mažas

footnotes: An attributive adjective normally precedes its noun, as in English.

rules.heading: Word Order
rules.statement: Because the endings show what each word is doing, word order is **freer than in English** and is used for emphasis rather than for grammar. The ordinary, unemphatic order is nevertheless subject – verb – predicate, and the learner should keep to it until the effect of departing from it is understood.

examples.note: emphatic; the same words, a different point

vocabulary.notes: Feminine although it ends in -is. Compare akis (eye), naktis (night), širdis (heart).

drills.stem: Which of these nouns is **feminine**?
drills.explanation: Ending -a marks feminine (¶11). -as and -is here are masculine; *brolis* is the tempting near-miss because -is *can* be feminine in a tiny closed class (*moteris*), but *brolis* is not in that class.

drills.stem: How many genders does Lithuanian distinguish for nouns?
drills.explanation: Two: masculine and feminine. There is no neuter (¶10). Answering 3 imports Latin/German/Russian.

drills.stem: Translate: **The book is new.**
drills.explanation: *knyga* is feminine, so the predicate adjective is *nauja* (¶17). *naujas* is masculine agreement error; *esu* is 1sg; *nėra* negates.

drills.stem: Which form of *būti* goes with **mes**?
drills.explanation: *mes esame*. *esate* is jūs; *esu* is aš; *yra* covers the whole third person singular and plural (¶15) — tempting if you think "plural = yra".

drills.stem: Which sentences show **correct** gender agreement?
drills.explanation: *didelis* (class III) matches masculine *namas*; *graži* (class II) matches feminine *mergaitė*. *Katė yra mažas* and *Brolis yra nauja* reverse gender (¶17). Class-II *graži* (not *graža*) is itself a near-miss pattern.

drills.stem: *Namas yra didelis* can mean both "a house is big" and "the house is big". Why?
options: Because the nominative case is ambiguous between the two.
Because Lithuanian has no articles, definite or indefinite.
Because the adjective follows the noun.
drills.explanation: No article exists (¶12). Definiteness is contextual or shown by a demonstrative. The other options describe real facts that do not explain the a/the ambiguity.

drills.stem: Which of these nouns are **masculine**?
drills.explanation: -as and -is mark masculines here; -ė and -a mark feminines (¶11). *brolis* is masculine despite the -is trap class.

drills.stem: *Moteris* ends in -is yet takes feminine adjectives. What does this show?
options: That gender always follows natural sex.
That -is is mostly masculine but has a small feminine class that must be memorised.
drills.explanation: Endings are a guide, not a law: *moteris, akis, naktis, širdis* are the closed feminine -is set (¶11). Option A overgeneralises; B fails for *stalas* (m.) etc.

drills.stem: **Mokytoja yra gera ir nauja.** If the subject became *mokytojas*, how many of the remaining words would change form?
drills.explanation: Two: *gera* → *geras* and *nauja* → *naujas* (¶16–¶17). *yra* and *ir* have no gender. Answering 3 wrongly genders the verb; answering 1 forgets the second adjective.

drills.stem: Translate: **The book is not new.**
drills.explanation: Third-person negative of *būti* is irregular **nėra**, one word (¶15). *neyra* and *ne yra* are spelling traps; *naujas* fails feminine agreement.

drills.stem: For the adjective **gražus**, which feminine forms are correct in the nominative?
drills.explanation: Class II is *-us / -i*: feminine nominative is *graži*, not *graža* (class I pattern) or *gražė* (class III pattern) (¶17). *gražus* is masculine.

drills.stem: Which ending typically marks a **masculine** nominative singular?
drills.explanation: ¶11: masculine dictionary forms end in -as/-is/-ys/-us; -a/-ė are feminine. *-os* is genitive feminine, not nominative.

drills.stem: Translate: **She is a teacher.**
drills.explanation: Predicate noun matches gender: *mokytoja* (¶16–¶17). *mokytojas* is masculine; *esu* is 1sg; *mokytoją* is accusative.

drills.stem: Which nouns are **feminine** by the usual ending guide?
drills.explanation: *-a/*-ė → feminine (¶11). *stalas* (-as) is masculine.

drills.stem: Which form of *būti* goes with **jie**?
drills.explanation: Third person *yra* serves singular and plural, both genders (¶15). *esame/esate* are 1pl/2pl; *esi* is 2sg.

drills.stem: Which sentences are well formed?
drills.explanation: Adjective agrees in gender (¶17): *didelis* with *namas*, *maža* with *katė*. *knyga…didelis* and *berniukas…maža* mismatch.

drills.stem: **Aš ____ mokytojas.** Which form fits?
drills.explanation: 1sg of *būti* is *esu* (¶15).

drills.stem: Which of these are **third-person nominative** pronouns?
drills.explanation: *jis*, *ji*, and *jie* are third person. *aš* is first person singular.

drills.stem: Why can *Tai namas* mean “This is a house” with no article?
options: Lithuanian has no articles; context decides
drills.explanation: ¶12: no articles; *tai* introduces/identifies but is not an article.

drills.stem: For **didelis**, which feminine nominative forms are correct?
drills.explanation: Class III: masc. *didelis* / fem. *didelė* (¶17). The other shapes are wrong or other cases.

drills.stem: *Brolis* ends in **-is**. Gender?
options: Masculine; ending is only a guide, and *brolis* is masc.
drills.explanation: ¶11: -is is usually masculine (*brolis*); *moteris* is a known feminine exception — endings nearly reliable, not absolute.

drills.stem: **Katė yra graži.** Change the subject to *namas*. How many of the other two words must change for agreement?
drills.explanation: *yra* is unchanged (3rd person one form). Only the adjective *graži* → *gražus* (¶15–¶17). Answering 2 wrongly changes *yra*.

drills.stem: The nominative is the case of the:
drills.explanation: ¶13: nominative = subject / dictionary form.

drills.stem: Which use **nominative** predicate nouns/adjectives correctly after *būti*?
drills.explanation: Predicate stands in nominative (¶16). *mažą* is accusative — wrong after *yra*.

drills.stem: **Mes ____ geri.**
drills.explanation: 1pl *esame* (¶15). *yra* is 3rd person only.

drills.title: Namas ir mokytojai
drills.passage: Tai namas. Namas yra didelis ir naujas. Čia yra Jonas. Jonas yra mokytojas. Jis yra geras mokytojas. Čia yra Rūta. Rūta yra mokytoja. Ji yra graži. Namas yra mokykla. Mergaitė yra maža, o berniukas yra didelis. Moteris yra gera. Knyga nėra nauja.
drills.translation: This is a house. The house is big and new. Here is Jonas. Jonas is a teacher. He is a good teacher. Here is Rūta. Rūta is a teacher. She is beautiful. The house is a school. The girl is small, and the boy is big. The woman is good. The book is not new.

questions.explanation: *Jonas yra mokytojas* — masculine predicate noun. *mokytoja* is the feminine near-miss.

questions.stem: Which statements about **namas** does the passage support?
questions.explanation: Big, new, and a school. *Namas yra maža* is unsupported and wrongly feminine.

questions.stem: In how many sentences is the thing asserted of the subject a bare **predicate adjective** (not a noun, and not an attributive adjective inside a noun phrase)?
questions.explanation: Five sentences: *Namas yra didelis ir naujas*; *Ji yra graži*; *Mergaitė yra maža, o berniukas yra didelis* (one sentence, two clauses); *Moteris yra gera*; *Knyga nėra nauja*. Trap: *Jis yra geras mokytojas* — the predicate is the noun *mokytojas*; *geras* is only attributive (¶16–¶17). Answering 6 double-counts the coordinated *Mergaitė… berniukas…* sentence.

questions.stem: Why is *Moteris yra gera* well formed despite the ending **-is**?
options: Because *moteris* belongs to the closed feminine -is class, so adjectives are feminine.
Because *gera* agrees with natural sex only, never with grammatical gender.
questions.explanation: *moteris* is the textbook feminine -is noun (¶11); *gera* follows grammatical gender, not a special sex rule.

questions.stem: Which forms of *būti* appear in the passage?
questions.explanation: Affirmative *yra* throughout and negative *nėra* in *Knyga nėra nauja*. First-person forms do not appear.
